title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 2 (Part 2) Virtual Human and Digital Fashion
description: The second part of the CLO Official Academic Month Video Episode 2 is here! Specially invited is a professor from the William De Kooning School of Art and Design to share the application of CLO in teaching, adopting a "bidirectional parallel" approach to cultivate future talents in the fashion industry with design thinking that integrates virtual and physical elements!
transcript:
Okay, Annette, Leroy, we are very excited to hear more about your program and how CLO has been used.  
So I'm handing over to you.  
You can start whenever you are ready.  

Okay, thank you, Elaine.  
Yes, we are ready.  

Okay, so hello everyone, and today Leroy and I will talk to you about education, our education in virtual fashion design at our school, the Willem de Kooning Academy in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.  
First, let me briefly explain how our institute is structured.  
We have students who enter our school in their major.  
There are many design majors to choose from, such as graphic design, advertising, and in our case, fashion design.  
To educate our students in skills, we have our stations, or you could also call them workplaces, such as the print station, the metal workstation, and the fabric station, or the textile workplace, as you can see here on the screen.  
All our workplaces and stations can be used by all our students, which encourages cross-disciplinary work.  
Of course, our fashion students will mostly be found in the fabric station.  
But when teaching virtual fashion design, they will also be found mostly in the fabric station.  
So we need expertise from many stations.  
From the fabric station, we need tutors who specialize in patterns and virtual pattern making.  
From our image and sound station, we need tutors skilled in making animations or games, who can teach programs like Blender and 3D Coat.  
And in our interaction station, there are people specialized in VR and AR presentations who teach students how to work in Gravity Sketch or, for example, how to print in 3D.  
That, I think, is what makes our school quite unique.  
It enables students, after being trained in the necessary basic low-level 3D skills that are closely related to fashion, patterns, and fabrics, to explore with these acquired skills a whole new world of different kinds of mostly interdisciplinary projects in their own field of interest.  
We have students who explore virtual materials.  
We have students who focus on virtual image making, on fashion in games, or on digital film.  
We are not just educating for the fashion industry today, but much more for the creative industry of tomorrow.  

Leroy.  

Yes, hello.  
My name is Leroy, and I am going to talk a little about one of the research projects we are conducting around virtual fashion.  
Because to keep up with the rapid changes in fashion, we need to focus on what we are doing in the digital world.  
We need to look at the digital world as a whole.  
But in the context of our creative industry, we as an academy are always looking for new perspectives and cutting-edge technologies to become a better version of ourselves.  
In this light, since last year we have been working on the Erasmus Plus research project Me, You, Us in collaboration with design schools in Kolding, Denmark, and the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia.  
In this research project, we are searching for new methodologies to educate fashion design using digital tools and virtual reality.  
Here Clo3D is one of our main programs that we use.  
However, virtual fashion design is not something new at Willem de Kooning Academy.  
We started our virtual journey with Clo3D already back in 2018 when we were introduced to the program at PI Apparel in Berlin.  
At that time, we saw the potential of Clo3D, especially as something practical—let's say another way of expressing physical design.  
However, in recent years, we have been learning together with our students and have concluded that there is so much more potential in virtual design beyond being just an extension of physical fashion design.  
We came to understand that the virtual design world also needs a virtual design ontology—in other words, a virtual way of understanding the virtual world itself as well as the physical world around us.  
Perhaps it is in our Dutch nature, but it seems very logical to us that a tool like Clo3D or any other kind of virtual design software could also be used as a critical design tool.  
This critical perspective also stands at the core of the ME-US research project.  
The research is built on three pillars that we call our CIT goals, which stand for sustainability, inclusivity, and diversity.  
Together with these other schools, we are exploring what these urgent themes mean today and what these themes will mean in the future of virtual fashion design.  
We are still very early in the research phase, but we would love to take you along in our research later on.  

Okay, yeah, I'll take it from here again because today we really want to share the work of our students, rather than just telling how we do things and how we run things.  
So while we are talking, we will show student work.  
For us, creativity and artistic development of our students takes center stage, and therefore we do not just focus on the technical advances of the program Clo3D, but rather on its creative potential.  
And to be clear, we, the Willem de Kooning Academy, are not a fashion institute.  
We do not feel obliged to educate ready-to-go fashion professionals who will inevitably all work in the current fashion industry.  
Of course, they might choose to do so, and we support them in that too, of course.  
But that is not our full intention.  
We are an art school that trains fully-rounded creatives who might later in life become fashion designers.  
For us, a good student knows how to use their creativity to set action in motion, and to use design as a means to tell a story, to be critical of the world around them, and to be part of the solution rather than the problem.  
Therefore, we train them to, firstly, work sufficiently in Clo3D to visualize their designs, but also at the same time we challenge them to hack the program and use Clo3D to challenge society’s notions of fashion.  
This is very exciting to us.  
It might be our rebellious Dutch nature, but we like to challenge the parameters of systems and to disturb existing hierarchies and see what lies beyond the known.  
To us, it is a system embedded in fashion to challenge the current state of fashion.  
To do this, we have embedded Clo3D in three of the four years of our fashion bachelor course, with a possible fourth year when a student chooses to use Clo3D for their graduation project.  
Just like any other fashion course that uses Clo3D in its curriculum, we acknowledge there is still a great gap between physical making and the use of virtual prototyping.  
Leroy is one of the professors who uses Clo3D in his classes and who encounters this discrepancy.  
Leroy, could you tell a little more about how you try to bring physical making and virtual making together in your classes?  

Well, thank you, Annette.  
I will try to do so.  
It is indeed true that one of the biggest problems we face in our education with the shift towards virtual and digital design in our curriculum is the gap between physical and virtual making.  
From an outside perspective, this gap might seem insignificant, but it poses a real problem and a headache for us as a department.  
To be fully honest, we are still searching for answers and I cannot provide a full answer today.  
That is also why we are doing this research project.  
But I can say this: from our experience, we have learned that the divide between physical and virtual making is not just a question of technology that can be solved by one of the many features of the Clo3D program.  
For example, students can easily create patterns in Clo3D and print them to stitch their digital designs into physical samples.  
This is very easy for them and is not the problem.  
The actual problem lies much deeper—in the inner world of the students’ creativity and design intuition.  
Over the years, we have noticed that Clo3D was often seen as an additional skill next to their physical design practice.  
We still see a lot of skepticism from a more traditional corner of our fashion industry.  
Virtual making was just another way of expressing physical fashion design.  
We also still see these attitudes towards virtual design in many fashion institutes.  
Virtual design is often just an add-on in education, a nice way to present a physical dress that you could make for real.  
On the other hand, as an academy, we see that the next generation who grew up with the technology is already able to use tech as their second nature.  
In the Netherlands today, a six-year-old child often knows how to use a tablet before they know how to write.  
The future is clearly already here.  
At the Willem de Kooning Academy, we feel the need to respond to this rapidly changing world.  
Therefore, we have chosen to include virtual and digital communication in the basics of our fashion major education, right alongside physical skills.  
By simultaneously teaching students practical skills like pattern drawing in physical and virtual reality, we hope to annul this divide altogether by creating a parallel design intuition.  
We hope that by continuously switching back and forth between physical and virtual reality, students will no longer feel this division but see them as an extension of one another—one and the same thing.  
Well, that’s what we hope.  

Annette will now tell you how we do this in the first-year design assignment called Bending for Functionality.  
While I was talking, you can see the work of one of our students, Besa Demirci.  
Thanks.  

I think so.  
Now back to you.  

From the very first day that our students enter the fashion department, we introduce them to the idea of virtual technology.  
In fact, we have heard from students that they really choose our school for its virtual and digital approach to fashion.  
As we said, our major fashion design education is roughly three years, and we introduce virtual fashion methodologies in block 1.3—that is, in the first year, just before the summer holiday.  
Of course, we introduce digital technical skills like pattern drawing and the basics of clothes earlier in the year.  
But to guarantee an inclusive learning environment, we must presume that students still need to learn all these skills, even though some might already be very experienced in virtual pattern drawing.  
As mentioned before, these practical skills are taught at our school by our station instructors.  
For first-year students, these are Paulina Martina, who has a background in speculative VR design and is an expert on AI, and Geert van der Meer, who is a professional pattern drawer with great knowledge of digitizing patterns.  
When our students know the basics of both physical and virtual fashion design, our fashion design tutors come in.  
For the Bending for Functionality project, these are Selina Parr and Anouk van Klaveren.  
Together, they introduce our students to this parallel methodology of designing fashions.  

The focus of our first-year project is for students to learn to critically question the function of everyday garments.  
They start this research in the physical realm with Selina Parr and in Clo3D with Anouk van Klaveren.  
In the physical starting class, they dissect an iconic garment and question its functionality through physical methods.  
This could be through draping the garment, cutting it up, making collages, sketching on paper—just physical ways of expressing a design.  
Then, quite traditionally, they sample this garment in calico, for which they must make the pattern by hand on paper.  
Only then do they digitize the paper patterns into Clo3D and make a 3D render of their design.  
Because there is a physical calico sample at that time, the tutors can really compare this virtual 3D model to its physical calico counterpart.  
This provides the tutors and instructors with an actual reference to measure the 3D garment against.  

While all this happens simultaneously with Selina’s classes, in Anouk’s classes, students start with a virtual garment that they morph, dissect, and transform using the tools in Clo3D.  
We try to cultivate the same curiosity and spontaneity in virtual space as our students have in the physical assignments.  
Although students are playing around with patterns in the 2D box of Clo3D, physical makeability is not a concern in this virtual exploratory phase.  
Students first need to visualize their ideas in virtual space.  
In the second half of the semester, they adapt these virtual designs into makeable patterns that can be printed and executed in fabric.  
With one tutor, students go from physical to virtual; with the other, they go from virtual to physical.  
These processes run in parallel.  
At any given point in this project, they are working on each segment both in physical space and in virtual space simultaneously.  

I will continue with year two.  
The second-year project is called Future of Fashion.  
I have a few videos to show in the meantime because they are working on animations.  

The Future of Fashion project primarily focuses on the power of speculation in fashion design and virtual fashion design as a device for storytelling.  
The brief to our students is quite simple: come up with a future scenario of the world and design a virtual collection that represents this speculative scenario.  
The final project of Future of Fashion is an animation showcasing this digital collection in a self-created virtual environment.  
Here we see the work of Zala Meshan.  
Guiding this project are Sreena Parr on the collection design front and Esther van Brake, who is actually an alumna of Willem de Kooning Academy and graduated in 2017 with a virtual fashion project. She now teaches concept development.  
Natalia van Coren focuses on circular economies and sustainability in this project.  

What we hope to do in this project is not only focus on the problems of the world today—which is quite easy; you only have to look outside to see them—but we ask students to speculate about the problems of tomorrow from the perspective of today.  
For some students, this means coming up with solution-driven concepts to battle impacts such as rising sea levels or reducing biodiversity.  
Other students use this Future of Fashion project as a platform for social commentary, through grotesque exaggeration and humor, designing a parody of contemporary culture.  
For example, here we see the project of Philip Malmgren, who really explores the parameters and limitations of the Clo3D program by making a kind of parody out of it.  

On a more practical skill-based level, we want to teach students how to seamlessly switch between different software and methods of making digital images.  
Again, we want to cultivate a digital intuition in our students and provide different ways of making digital images to contribute to this.  
For example, students design and make their clothes in Clo3D.  
They create environments and virtual worlds in Blender, and also sculpt accessories in Gravity Sketch or Rhino.  
In the end, they use a multitude of different engines to bring their animation videos to life.  

This is all highly technical and somewhat beyond the technical capabilities of our fashion tutors—and also beyond my own technical capabilities.  
At Willem de Kooning Academy, we are very lucky to have stations with plenty of expert knowledge on Clo3D programming and virtual design methods.  
For this project, we work closely with the Image and Sound Station, represented by Peter Schropp, who specializes in animations and games, and with the Interaction Station, represented by Brigitte Lichtenegger, Joris Butter, and Mike Pelletier, all experts in AR, VR, and interaction design.  

The last part is the year three part.  
The last real assignment in our fashion design major we call the major assignment, partly due to its enormous size, but also because all the knowledge the students have obtained so far accumulates in this project.  
It is also the moment when students really have to start thinking about professionalization in preparation for their internships in the second half of the third year.  
We believe that with professionalization comes a great degree of specialization.  
We acknowledge that our program can be very demanding for our students.  
Therefore, we ask them to choose either a physical track, where they focus on making a physical collection, or a virtual track, where they work on an immersive virtual fashion experience.  
By this time, students already know much better what their strengths are, and they quite naturally choose according to their preference.  

The choice to split the course into physical and virtual is because we believe that in this year of professionalization, it should be up to the student to choose what they want to specialize in.  
By this time, the station classes have become so incredibly expert that we acknowledge they are only useful for those who really want to continue in virtual fashion design.  
However, we see an increasing demand and interest from our students to follow these classes.  
Although we make a division between physical and virtual projects, these two tracks really start off together in an extensive conceptual phase.  
As we said before, we believe the design process of physical and virtual fashion is the same; they only diverge in technical execution.  

The fashion tutors assigned to this project are Leroy van Halen, who is sitting next to me here and who, besides teaching, also works as a fashion designer for Parisian luxury brands, and Anouk van Klaveren, who also has an experimental fashion-based practice focusing on exhibitions and fashion in the public context.  

Yes, thank you, Annette.  
As you saw, a few examples of projects that we did.  
In this assignment, we do very expert, immersive virtual fashion experiences.  
We want to show you one particular project.  
This project is from Nino van Litt.  
Nino is a student of ours who manages to come up with a very unique perspective of what he wants and uses all different kinds of platforms to make, in the end, a game.  
He made the clothes, which are very speculative garments, for example in Clo3D.  
He started digitally by using a lot of digital materials.  
His collection is about stock image and digital material culture, which he then imported into designs made in Clo3D.  
He used many different engines and programs, but predominantly Unity, to make a playable game out of it.  

We are going to show you a little video about his game.  
In the corner, you see the student himself.  

Hey, what's up, guys? It's Scarce here.  
Today, I hope you're doing well.  
It's time for a reaction to an interesting post, a thought piece I saw on the internet on our subreddit.  
Huge holidays.  
Look it up.  
Chris, where are you going?  
Oh my God.  
What is going on?  
Going to take a few hours to get 20K?  
Oh, you bet your ass it will, yeah.  
Adequate for 20K.  
That's a bad guy.  
When he comes into my shop, he causes trouble.  
Rolling 80 of these is going to be the biggest pain in the ass.  
Oh my God.  
Yeah, baby.  
That's what I've been waiting for.  
That's what it's all about.  

Here you can really see what we like to show our students.  
Of course, Clo3D at our academy starts very much off where you saw kind of expression of design, but there are so many more opportunities in a much more creative sense to use this program.  
All the garments and statues in this gallery space were created in Clo3D, but only using this program as a segment in a much bigger creative process.  

Thanks, Leroy.  
And thank you all for listening.  

At Willem de Kooning Academy, our aim is to break down the digital divide, and we have entered a digital reality.  
At WDKA, we are in this together.  
So in our Erasmus project, Me, You, Us, the research project, we study the interaction between the physical and the virtual, the old and the new skills, the traditions and the possible futures.  

I hope all the student work you saw in the last half hour has inspired you.  
It certainly continues to inspire us.  
Thank you.

chunks.content: ## Education in Virtual Fashion Design at Willem de Kooning Academy This section outlines the structure and interdisciplinary approach of the Willem de Kooning Academy's fashion design program, emphasizing the integration of virtual fashion design using tools like Clo3D alongside traditional physical fashion education. The Willem de Kooning Academy in Rotterdam, Netherlands, offers multiple design majors, including fashion design. The school is organized into various specialized workstations—such as print, metal, fabric (textile), image and sound, and interaction stations—that students from all majors can access. This structure encourages cross-disciplinary collaboration. Fashion students primarily use the fabric station but also benefit from expertise in virtual pattern making, animation, 3D modeling, VR, AR, and 3D printing, taught by specialists in the corresponding stations. This approach equips students with foundational 3D skills related to fashion, patterns, and fabrics, enabling exploration of virtual materials, digital image making, fashion in gaming, and digital film. The academy’s focus is not limited to preparing students for the current fashion industry but aims to train creatives for the future’s broader creative industries by merging traditional and digital techniques. --- ## Research Project: Me, You, Us and Virtual Fashion Methodologies This section covers the Erasmus Plus research project "Me, You, Us," which explores new educational methodologies in virtual fashion design, focusing on sustainability, inclusivity, and diversity using Clo3D and virtual reality tools. Since 2022, the Willem de Kooning Academy has collaborated with design schools in Kolding, Denmark, and Ljubljana, Slovenia, on the Erasmus Plus project "Me, You, Us." The project investigates innovative ways to teach fashion design with digital tools and virtual reality, using Clo3D as a primary software. The academy's virtual fashion journey began in 2018 with Clo3D, recognizing it initially as a practical extension of physical fashion design. However, recent insights show virtual design holds greater potential as a critical design tool, requiring a virtual design ontology—a conceptual framework to understand virtual and physical worlds in tandem. The project’s core pillars, abbreviated as CIT, stand for sustainability, inclusivity, and diversity. These themes are examined for their current and future implications in virtual fashion design. Although the research is in early stages, the academy intends to share ongoing findings and developments. --- ## Educational Philosophy: Creativity Over Technical Mastery This section explains the academy’s pedagogical approach, prioritizing student creativity and critical thinking over purely technical skill with Clo3D, and how students are encouraged to use virtual fashion as a medium for societal critique. The Willem de Kooning Academy positions itself as an art school rather than a traditional fashion institute. It trains broadly creative individuals, not just ready-to-work fashion professionals. Students are taught to use design to tell stories, question societal norms, and contribute to solutions. Clo3D is embedded throughout three years of the fashion bachelor curriculum, with students optionally using it for their graduation project. The academy encourages students not just to use Clo3D for visualization but to "hack" the software and challenge fashion’s existing systems and hierarchies, reflecting a rebellious and experimental Dutch approach to design.

chunks.content: It trains broadly creative individuals, not just ready-to-work fashion professionals. Students are taught to use design to tell stories, question societal norms, and contribute to solutions. Clo3D is embedded throughout three years of the fashion bachelor curriculum, with students optionally using it for their graduation project. The academy encourages students not just to use Clo3D for visualization but to "hack" the software and challenge fashion’s existing systems and hierarchies, reflecting a rebellious and experimental Dutch approach to design. --- ## Bridging Physical and Virtual Fashion Making This section addresses the ongoing challenge of integrating physical garment making with virtual design practices and the academy’s strategy to develop a parallel design intuition bridging both worlds. One major challenge is the gap between physical and virtual making. While students can easily create digital patterns in Clo3D and print them for physical samples, the deeper issue is integrating virtual design into students’ creative intuition. Traditionally, virtual design was viewed as an add-on to physical design, with skepticism persisting in many fashion education settings. However, younger generations embrace digital technology naturally. The academy aims to teach physical and virtual pattern-making simultaneously, encouraging students to switch fluidly between realities. This parallel approach aspires to dissolve the division so students perceive physical and virtual design as extensions of one another. --- ## Year 1: Bending for Functionality Project This section details the first-year design assignment focusing on critical analysis of garment functionality through simultaneous physical and virtual design practices using Clo3D. From day one, first-year fashion students are introduced to virtual technology. Virtual fashion methodologies begin in the first year’s Block 1.3 (just before summer), after learning basic physical and digital pattern skills. Students work under tutors specializing in speculative VR and AI (Paulina Martina) and professional pattern drawing/digitization (Geert van der Meer). Fashion tutors Selina Parr and Anouk van Klaveren lead the "Bending for Functionality" project, which teaches a parallel design methodology. Students start by physically dissecting and analyzing an iconic garment—draping, cutting, sketching, and making calico samples from hand-drawn patterns. They then digitize paper patterns into Clo3D for 3D rendering, allowing direct comparison between physical and virtual samples. Concurrently, students explore virtual garments in Clo3D by morphing and transforming patterns without immediate concern for physical makeability. The second semester focuses on adapting virtual designs into practical, makeable patterns. The entire process encourages working simultaneously in physical and virtual spaces. --- ## Year 2: Future of Fashion Project This section explains the second-year project that emphasizes speculative storytelling in virtual fashion design, integrating multiple digital tools and interdisciplinary collaboration. The second-year project, "Future of Fashion," centers on speculative design and storytelling through virtual fashion collections. Students create future world scenarios and design digital collections representing these speculative futures. The project culminates in animations showcasing their collections within virtual environments. Students receive guidance from tutors specializing in collection design (Sreena Parr), concept development (alumna Esther van Brake), and sustainability (Natalia van Coren).

chunks.content: --- ## Year 2: Future of Fashion Project This section explains the second-year project that emphasizes speculative storytelling in virtual fashion design, integrating multiple digital tools and interdisciplinary collaboration. The second-year project, "Future of Fashion," centers on speculative design and storytelling through virtual fashion collections. Students create future world scenarios and design digital collections representing these speculative futures. The project culminates in animations showcasing their collections within virtual environments. Students receive guidance from tutors specializing in collection design (Sreena Parr), concept development (alumna Esther van Brake), and sustainability (Natalia van Coren). Projects range from solution-driven concepts addressing future environmental challenges to social commentary using exaggeration and parody, such as Philip Malmgren’s work exploring Clo3D’s limits humorously. Technically, students use Clo3D for garment design, Blender for virtual world creation, Gravity Sketch or Rhino for accessories, and various engines to animate final videos. The academy collaborates closely with the Image and Sound Station (Peter Schropp) and the Interaction Station (Brigitte Lichtenegger, Joris Butter, Mike Pelletier) for expertise in animation, games, AR, VR, and interaction design. --- ## Year 3: Major Assignment and Specialization Tracks This section covers the third-year culminating project where students choose specialized tracks—physical or virtual—and apply accumulated knowledge toward professionalization and internship preparation. The final major assignment in the third year consolidates students’ accumulated skills and serves as preparation for internships. Students choose between two tracks: - **Physical track:** Focus on creating a tangible fashion collection. - **Virtual track:** Develop immersive virtual fashion experiences. This choice reflects students’ recognized strengths and interests, with the assumption that professionalization requires specialization. Although the tracks diverge technically, both begin with a shared, extensive conceptual phase, reinforcing the academy’s belief that design processes are fundamentally the same, diverging only in execution. Tutors for this project include Leroy van Halen, an active designer for Parisian luxury brands, and Anouk van Klaveren, who has an experimental fashion practice focused on exhibitions and public fashion. --- ## Example Project: Nino van Litt’s Immersive Virtual Fashion Game This section presents a case study of a student project that integrates Clo3D, digital materials, and game development platforms to create a unique virtual fashion experience. Student Nino van Litt created an immersive virtual fashion project combining speculative garment design and interactive gaming. Using Clo3D, he designed speculative digital garments inspired by stock image and digital material culture. He integrated these designs into a playable game developed mainly in Unity, incorporating various digital engines and platforms. The project exemplifies the academy’s encouragement to use Clo3D not just as a design tool but as part of a broader creative and technical workflow. --- ## Conclusion: Bridging Physical and Virtual Realities in Fashion Education Willem de Kooning Academy is committed to bridging the gap between physical and virtual fashion design through interdisciplinary education, research, and creative experimentation. Their Erasmus project "Me, You, Us" continues to explore the interaction between physical and virtual skills, traditions, and futures in fashion.

Their Erasmus project "Me, You, Us" continues to explore the interaction between physical and virtual skills, traditions, and futures in fashion. The academy’s approach fosters a new generation of creatives equipped to navigate and shape the evolving digital reality in fashion, emphasizing sustainability, inclusivity, diversity, and critical engagement with technology. --- # Terminology and Technologies Highlighted - **Clo3D:** 3D fashion design and virtual prototyping software. - **Blender:** Open-source 3D creation suite used for environment and virtual world building. - **Gravity Sketch:** 3D design software, often used for VR modeling. - **Rhino:** 3D modeling software, used for accessories. - **Unity:** Game engine used to create interactive virtual fashion experiences. - **VR (Virtual Reality) and AR (Augmented Reality):** Technologies used to present and interact with virtual fashion. - **Erasmus Plus "Me, You, Us":** Research project focused on digital methods in fashion education. - **Bending for Functionality:** First-year project integrating physical and virtual garment analysis and design. - **Future of Fashion:** Second-year project focusing on speculative virtual fashion storytelling. - **CIT Goals:** Sustainability, Inclusivity, and Diversity in virtual fashion design education. --- This document captures the detailed educational structure, research initiatives, project methodologies, and creative philosophies of Willem de Kooning Academy's virtual fashion design program, providing a comprehensive resource for semantic search and vector-based retrieval in the domain of digital fashion education.

However, recent insights show virtual design holds greater potential as a critical design tool, requiring a virtual design ontology—a conceptual framework to understand virtual and physical worlds in tandem. The project’s core pillars, abbreviated as CIT, stand for sustainability, inclusivity, and diversity. These themes are examined for their current and future implications in virtual fashion design. Although the research is in early stages, the academy intends to share ongoing findings and developments. --- ## Educational Philosophy: Creativity Over Technical Mastery This section explains the academy’s pedagogical approach, prioritizing student creativity and critical thinking over purely technical skill with Clo3D, and how students are encouraged to use virtual fashion as a medium for societal critique. The Willem de Kooning Academy positions itself as an art school rather than a traditional fashion institute. It trains broadly creative individuals, not just ready-to-work fashion professionals. Students are taught to use design to tell stories, question societal norms, and contribute to solutions. Clo3D is embedded throughout three years of the fashion bachelor curriculum, with students optionally using it for their graduation project. The academy encourages students not just to use Clo3D for visualization but to "hack" the software and challenge fashion’s existing systems and hierarchies, reflecting a rebellious and experimental Dutch approach to design. --- ## Bridging Physical and Virtual Fashion Making This section addresses the ongoing challenge of integrating physical garment making with virtual design practices and the academy’s strategy to develop a parallel design intuition bridging both worlds. One major challenge is the gap between physical and virtual making. While students can easily create digital patterns in Clo3D and print them for physical samples, the deeper issue is integrating virtual design into students’ creative intuition. Traditionally, virtual design was viewed as an add-on to physical design, with skepticism persisting in many fashion education settings. However, younger generations embrace digital technology naturally. The academy aims to teach physical and virtual pattern-making simultaneously, encouraging students to switch fluidly between realities. This parallel approach aspires to dissolve the division so students perceive physical and virtual design as extensions of one another. --- ## Year 1: Bending for Functionality Project This section details the first-year design assignment focusing on critical analysis of garment functionality through simultaneous physical and virtual design practices using Clo3D. From day one, first-year fashion students are introduced to virtual technology. Virtual fashion methodologies begin in the first year’s Block 1.3 (just before summer), after learning basic physical and digital pattern skills. Students work under tutors specializing in speculative VR and AI (Paulina Martina) and professional pattern drawing/digitization (Geert van der Meer). Fashion tutors Selina Parr and Anouk van Klaveren lead the "Bending for Functionality" project, which teaches a parallel design methodology. Students start by physically dissecting and analyzing an iconic garment—draping, cutting, sketching, and making calico samples from hand-drawn patterns. They then digitize paper patterns into Clo3D for 3D rendering, allowing direct comparison between physical and virtual samples. Concurrently, students explore virtual garments in Clo3D by morphing and transforming patterns without immediate concern for physical makeability. The second semester focuses on adapting virtual designs into practical, makeable patterns. The entire process encourages working simultaneously in physical and virtual spaces. --- ## Year 2: Future of Fashion Project This section explains the second-year project that emphasizes speculative storytelling in virtual fashion design, integrating multiple digital tools and interdisciplinary collaboration. The second-year project, "Future of Fashion," centers on speculative design and storytelling through virtual fashion collections. Students create future world scenarios and design digital collections representing these speculative futures. The project culminates in animations showcasing their collections within virtual environments. Students receive guidance from tutors specializing in collection design (Sreena Parr), concept development (alumna Esther van Brake), and sustainability (Natalia van Coren). Projects range from solution-driven concepts addressing future environmental challenges to social commentary using exaggeration and parody, such as Philip Malmgren’s work exploring Clo3D’s limits humorously. Technically, students use Clo3D for garment design, Blender for virtual world creation, Gravity Sketch or Rhino for accessories, and various engines to animate final videos. The academy collaborates closely with the Image and Sound Station (Peter Schropp) and the Interaction Station (Brigitte Lichtenegger, Joris Butter, Mike Pelletier) for expertise in animation, games, AR, VR, and interaction design. --- ## Year 3: Major Assignment and Specialization Tracks This section covers the third-year culminating project where students choose specialized tracks—physical or virtual—and apply accumulated knowledge toward professionalization and internship preparation. The final major assignment in the third year consolidates students’ accumulated skills and serves as preparation for internships. Students choose between two tracks: - **Physical track:** Focus on creating a tangible fashion collection. - **Virtual track:** Develop immersive virtual fashion experiences. This choice reflects students’ recognized strengths and interests, with the assumption that professionalization requires specialization. Although the tracks diverge technically, both begin with a shared, extensive conceptual phase, reinforcing the academy’s belief that design processes are fundamentally the same, diverging only in execution. Tutors for this project include Leroy van Halen, an active designer for Parisian luxury brands, and Anouk van Klaveren, who has an experimental fashion practice focused on exhibitions and public fashion. --- ## Example Project: Nino van Litt’s Immersive Virtual Fashion Game This section presents a case study of a student project that integrates Clo3D, digital materials, and game development platforms to create a unique virtual fashion experience. Student Nino van Litt created an immersive virtual fashion project combining speculative garment design and interactive gaming. Using Clo3D, he designed speculative digital garments inspired by stock image and digital material culture. He integrated these designs into a playable game developed mainly in Unity, incorporating various digital engines and platforms. The project exemplifies the academy’s encouragement to use Clo3D not just as a design tool but as part of a broader creative and technical workflow. --- ## Conclusion: Bridging Physical and Virtual Realities in Fashion Education Willem de Kooning Academy is committed to bridging the gap between physical and virtual fashion design through interdisciplinary education, research, and creative experimentation. Their Erasmus project "Me, You, Us" continues to explore the interaction between physical and virtual skills, traditions, and futures in fashion. The academy’s approach fosters a new generation of creatives equipped to navigate and shape the evolving digital reality in fashion, emphasizing sustainability, inclusivity, diversity, and critical engagement with technology. --- # Terminology and Technologies Highlighted - **Clo3D:** 3D fashion design and virtual prototyping software. - **Blender:** Open-source 3D creation suite used for environment and virtual world building. - **Gravity Sketch:** 3D design software, often used for VR modeling. - **Rhino:** 3D modeling software, used for accessories. - **Unity:** Game engine used to create interactive virtual fashion experiences. - **VR (Virtual Reality) and AR (Augmented Reality):** Technologies used to present and interact with virtual fashion. - **Erasmus Plus "Me, You, Us":** Research project focused on digital methods in fashion education. - **Bending for Functionality:** First-year project integrating physical and virtual garment analysis and design. - **Future of Fashion:** Second-year project focusing on speculative virtual fashion storytelling. - **CIT Goals:** Sustainability, Inclusivity, and Diversity in virtual fashion design education. --- This document captures the detailed educational structure, research initiatives, project methodologies, and creative philosophies of Willem de Kooning Academy's virtual fashion design program, providing a comprehensive resource for semantic search and vector-based retrieval in the domain of digital fashion education.
